summary: Repeatedly collect and remove all leaves of a binary tree; return the groups removed in each round.
mainInsight: A node is removed in the round equal to its height (leaves have height 1). A post-order DFS computes height = 1 + max(child heights) and appends the node to group[height - 1], with no actual removal.
invariant: When a node's height h is returned, groups[h - 1] already exists because one child has height h - 1 and was processed earlier.
canonicalApproach: Post-order DFS grouping nodes by height

approaches.name: Simulate removal
approaches.summary: Repeatedly traverse, collect leaves, detach them.

approaches.name: Post-order DFS grouping nodes by height
approaches.summary: Height from the bottom is the removal round.
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the output, O(h) stack

personalSolution.approach: Post-order DFS computing height and grouping values in a defaultdict keyed by height
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. mark.values() relies on dict insertion order; it is correct because height h is always first inserted before h + 1, but a list indexed by height - 1 makes the order explicit.

commonMistakes: Using depth from the root instead of height from the bottom.
Actually removing leaves round by round (correct but O(n * h)).
Off-by-one between height and list index.
edgeCases: Skewed tree -> n groups of one.
Perfect tree -> groups double in size toward the leaves.

cards.answer: Its height: 1 + max height of its children
cards.explanation: A node becomes a leaf once its tallest child subtree is gone, so it is removed in round 1 + max(child heights).

incorrectOptionExplanations.Its depth: distance from the root: Leaves at different depths are removed together in round 1.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Its number of descendants: A long chain and a bushy subtree with the same size need different rounds.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The round its parent is removed, minus o: Siblings can have different heights, so this is not determined by the parent.

cards.explanation: Heights are 3 (node 1), 2 (node 2), 1 (node 3): one node per round, bottom first.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[3, 2, 1]]: Only 3 is a leaf in round 1.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[3], [2, 1]]: Node 1 still has child 2 in round 2.

promptVariants: Your code returns list(mark.values()). Why are the groups in the right order?
Is returning the dict's values in insertion order safe here?
cards.answer: Yes. Python dicts keep insertion order, and height h is always inserted before height h + 1: a node of height h + 1 has a child of height h, and post-order processes the child first. So values() lists heights 1, 2, 3, ... in order. A list indexed by h - 1 makes this explicit.
keyPoints: Child of height h is processed before parent of h + 1
List by index is more explicit
cards.explanation: Relying on an ordering guarantee is fine if you can argue why it holds.
cards.code:
def dfs(root):
    if not root:
        return 0
    left = dfs(root.left)
    right = dfs(root.right)
    height = max(left, right) + 1
    mark[height].append(root.val)
    return height
dfs(root)
return [leaves for leaves in mark.values()]
